messages.body_plain:
On Sat, 2016-07-30 at 03:27 -0700, mahsa nadifar wrote:
>
>
>
> ,Hi
> :I'm attempting to compute MSE of parameters for my simulated data,
> based on gamma-count, Poisson and nbinomial distributions. But after
> some repetitions (at most 8th repetition), I got this error
>

the main issue is that the experiemnt is badly designed giving also
extreme counts.

the gammacount likelihood is computed as log(CDF(y+1..,)-CDF(y...,))
 and this might fail for high counts like yours.

you see this also for all the NAN/INF warnings you get in the output.

although its possible to replace the above with an asymptotic expansion
for large y, which goes like -n*y*a/b + constant(a,b), your problem
will remain.

see if you can set the simulation values so that somewhat more
reasonable values for dd$y are obtained.

H

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] INLA prediction
messages.body_plain:
Hi Andrea,

Can you provide a summary(result)?

One thing that can be going wrong is that your time parameter is near correlation = 1, so that your inference results says "this is static in time".

Another thing could be a coding error in predictions. How do you do predictions?

The third thing I can think of is that the result is actually correct. The prediction "mean" is the best guess for the future field values. And the field values for the last year of the study (2015) is a pretty good "best guess" for future years. What should change anyway is that you see the prediction variances increase into the future.

Kind regards,
Haakon

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I am working on a model with three regressions (three correlated dependent variables) that are estimated simultaneously and have different independent variables for each regression. They are seemingly unrelated regressions (SUR).
As the estimation through MCMC is taking more time than expected, I would like to know whether I can use INLA as an alternative and if R-INLA allows such kind of estimation.
The examples using R-INLA that I've seen so far usually work only with one regression.

Thanks in advance!

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Estimate two or more regressions parameters with INLA
messages.body_plain:
Hi,

Yes, from what the Wikipedia entry on SURs indicates, one possibility is to model the correlated measurement errors with an "iid3d" latent model. The details of course depend on the details of the model you have, but hopefully this should get you started. As a first step I recommend that you figure out the mathematical definition of your desired model; "shortcut names" like SUR won't tell you directly what a model really looks like.
See the latent models documentation on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org>.

Finn

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Estimate two or more regressions parameters with INLA
messages.body_plain:
Finn has already pointed out the iid3d latent model for the error
structure. For the rest, the simplest (but not very elegant) approach
might be to set covariates to the intercept value if they are not
needed, e.g. if you mean-centre everything then set unneeded
continuous covariates to 0, and factors to the first level. You might
want to be careful with the priors: I don't know how sensitive INLA
will be to integrating over vague priors.

An alternative would be to set out the model with a bit more care,
using some of the ideas here: <http://www.r-inla.org/models/tools>.
But unless you're going to be doing more complex stuff in the future,
this might be more hassle than its worth.

Bob

messages.subject_clean: [r-inla] Spatial autocorrelation in the SPDE approach
messages.body_plain:
Hi Nicola,

Are you familiar with other computational methods for dealing with spatial autocorrelation? For example direct use of a covariance model? The spde method in inla is a more computationally efficient alternative for solving the same problem for a specific family of covariances, namely the Matern family of covariances. This means that from a modelling point of view, the spde method is equivalent (up to some approximation differences) to several other spatial statistics methods, so if you're familiar with any of those that might help to explain it.  If you haven't done any spatial statistics at all, you may need to read more of the fundamental literature. Since you're doing epidemiology, the new book by Blangiardo and Cameletti may be a good place to look, since it does precisely that, using inla and SPDEs.

Book link:
https://books.google.co.uk/books?id=--HuBgAAQBAJ&dq=blangiardo+Cameletti&lr=&source=gbs_navlinks_s

Finn

Autocovariance, yes. messages.body_plain:
In the newst testing version, there is 'lognormalsurv' for the survival
lognormal, and 'lognormal' for the regression lognormal. so you can do

n = 300
x = runif(n)
eta = 1+x
y = exp(rnorm(n, mean = eta,  sd = 1))
data = list(y=y, event=rep(1, n), x=x)
formula = inla.surv(y, event) ~ 1 + x
r=inla(formula, family ="lognormalsurv", data=data)
summary(r)

data = data.frame(y, x)
formula = y  ~ 1 + x
r=inla(formula, family ="lognormal", data=data)
summary(r)

and the results should be the same.

H

Yes, I think that it is similar to perform the unconditional Poisson model as specified in formula 3 (that can be easily implemented with INLA). But this model fits a parameter (intercept) for each stratum and with conditional poisson model it is not necessary. As you can see in the table 4, to solve the same problem with Unconditional Poisson model have to be fitted 421 parameters while with Conditional poisson only 2 parameters are estimated. This is very important for me, because I want to perform a multiple time series analysis, where the number of parameters to be estimated with unconditional poisson could be very large and its estimation could be (computationally) impossible.

Perhaps including a constraint in the intercepts of the uncionditional Poisson model could be equivalent to the conditional poisson... I don't know...

Thank you!

It sounds like you're asking for something that would be relevant for an MCMC run, and not a direct calculation like INLA. On 8 Aug 2016, at 23:00, Gustavo Machado <gusta...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thank you very much, yes I have a discuss with people that are in MCMC but since we have this large data we can not fit in BUGS.

That's not what I meant. What I meant was that the entire concept of "check the model fit by looking at the mcmc trace plots to see if the MCMC chain has converged and is mixing well" is a question about an MCMC algorithm, and is not a relevant question when using the INLA method for Bayesian inference, so if someone requests that for INLA they most likely do not understand what INLA does, and/or that "Bayesian" is not synonymous with "MCMC".

> How could I get in this place the the optimization (residuals and gradient) from the model above? in order to converse my college that my model is doing ok?

The optimization diagnostics can be found in the verbose output; look for lines with "gradient" for example. But that only tells you something if you know how numerical optimization works, and doesn't usually tell you much at all about if your model fit is ok.

So, are you looking for evidence showing that the numerical algorithm has converged to the correct answer to the stated question (the posterior distributions for your specified model), or evidence that your model-data fit is good? Those are two very different questions, and the answer to the first one can be "yes" at the same time as the answer to the second question is "no" (the reverse can also happen, but is rare, and if it happens the results should generally not be trusted, since it is then unclear which question the algorithm has provided an answer to).

Finn

messages.subject: thinning of results
messages.subject_clean: thinning of results
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

It happens often to me that I end up handling quite large lists of
fitted models (e.g. for model comparison purposes).

INLA resulting objects can be quite heavy. Of course this depends
heavily on the model, the data, etc.

Currently I am packaging the results from a paper recently published [1]
for reproducibility. This involves fitting a few dozen models, whose
results add up to a few Gigabytes (!) in size.

I discovered that a good share of the size is contained in
`x$misc$configs`, which is not needed at all for the typical analysis of
results. At least for what I have used, which includes looking at
x$summary.* or x$marginals.*, using inla.?marginal() functions, and
inla.spde2.result().

This greatly reduces the size of the cached results. My question is
whether this is safe practice, and if there is any use case which is
hampered by this thinning.

Regards,

ƒacu.-

[1] http://dx.doi.org/10.1094/phyto-11-15-0284-r

Yes, I see the point.

its possible to do

r = inla(..., control.compute = list(return.marginals = FALSE))

which avoids the most memory issue, since all the marginals for the
latent field (although they are computed), are not returned to 'r',
only the summary statistics, like r$summary.fixed, etc. you'll still
have the marginals for the hyperpar, but they are only a few.

r$misc$configs  is only used if requested, and yes, this might take up
quite some mem. when not needed anymore, then you can just set it to
NULL.

hope this helps

messages.subject_clean: Mapping spatial effect with SPDE
messages.body_plain:
<https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-3HUsVKRnFPk/V6trOdZ7XuI/AAAAAAAACcY/j5Z37P1VJjUDdnOjR-prir_lqbrUP_rAwCLcB/s1600/heatmap_suffolkcounty_distorted.PNG>

Hello,

I am conducting a spatiotemporal analysis of binomial data observed on an island using the SPDE approach, and I am running into a strange error when attempting to map the spatial effect across my study area. I have cobbled together this approach from several guides and tutorials online, so apologies if there are any glaring omissions.

I've made my mesh from a polygon and a set of points, using unionSpatialPolygons and inla.sp2segment to turn the polygon into an inla.mesh.segment object for use in inla.mesh.create.helper.

loc<-cbind(DataWithDaymet$Long,DataWithDaymet$Lat) #Stores the lat/longs of each observation site
shape<-readOGR(dsn="LocationOfLayer", layer=("SuffolkPolygonDecDeg"))
ob <- unionSpatialPolygons(shape, rep(1, nrow(shape))) #This simplifies and unifies the boundary for faster processing
bound<-inla.sp2segment(ob) #Converts the polygon boundary to a inla.mesh.segment object, which is a series of line segments
(mesh<-inla.mesh.create.helper(points=cbind(DataWithDaymet$Long,DataWithDaymet$Lat),points.domain=bound$loc,offset=c(0.01,0.15),max.edge=c(0.1,0.2)))$n

Here is what the shapefile looks like with the observation locations printed on it:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-9BwXaX9esg0/V6tOcrdwXsI/AAAAAAAACcI/mN1T10Z3XfoOJOWg9Bfpde9BPZoBv9ipwCLcB/s1600/suffolk%2Bboundary%2Bwith%2Btrap%2Bpoints.PNG>

plot(mesh,asp=1)
lines(bound,lwd=2)
points(loc,cex=.75,pch=20,col=2)

Here is the mesh I am using, with the outline of the island my study is on superimposed in blue, and my observation points superimposed in red for reference:

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-kKMlRyUAKJg/V6tNFeminPI/AAAAAAAACb8/4awJRlK5rvYK16YfapPPj1SnLmQx31mEgCLcB/s1600/mesh%2Bwith%2Bborder%2Band%2Bpoints.PNG>

However, when I run the analysis using the following code:

A <-inla.spde.make.A(mesh, loc)
spde<-inla.spde2.matern(mesh,alpha=2)
formula<-Result ~ 0 + Intercept + AREIS_SepticCount1km + NDVI + Developed..Low.Intensity + Emergent.Herbaceous.Wetlands + WkMeanPrcp + WkMeanTmax + f(spatial, model=spde) #Defining the formula and variables
vars<-DataWithDaymet[,c(11,12,15,27,49,50)] #Takes out from the full dataset only the variables of interest mentioned in the formula
vars<-scale(vars)
stk<-inla.stack(data=list(Result=DataWithDaymet$Result),A=list(A,1),effect=list(list(spatial=1:spde$n.spde),data.frame(Intercept=1,vars)))  #Creating the stack for easy specification of INLA
r<-inla(formula, family="binomial", Ntrials=10596, data=inla.stack.data(stk), control.family=list(link="logit"), control.predictor=list(A=inla.stack.A(stk)),control.compute=list(dic=TRUE,cpo=TRUE)) #Running the INLA and checking marginals
summary(r)

and then use the following code to try and plot the spatial effect mean and SD onto the projector grid.

#Plotting the response on a grid
library(lattice)
projection<-inla.mesh.projector(mesh, dims=c(500,500)) #projects the mesh onto a square grid
table(xy.in <http://xy.in> <- inout(projection$lattice$loc,cbind(bound$loc[,1], bound$loc[,2]))) #Removes the grid points that are outside the boundary
#These are for the spatial field random effect, not the response
prd.m<-inla.mesh.project(projection,r$summary.ran$spatial$mean) #Projects the spatial effect mean onto the grid
prd.s<-inla.mesh.project(projection,r$summary.ran$spatial$s) #Projects the spatial effect SD onto the grid
prd.m[!xy.in <http://xy.in>] <- prd.s[!xy.in <http://xy.in>] <- NA #sets the projections outside the boundary to "NA"
library(gridExtra)
levelplot(prd.m, col.regions=terrain.colors(16))
levelplot(prd.s, col.regions=terrain.colors(16))

The resulting graph looks like this. My outline is chopped-up and distorted, despite using the boundary shapefile "bound" shown above which, when plotted, shows a normal shape. What might be causing this?

 <https://lh3.googleusercontent.com/-3HUsVKRnFPk/V6trOdZ7XuI/AAAAAAAACcY/j5Z37P1VJjUDdnOjR-prir_lqbrUP_rAwCLcB/s1600/heatmap_suffolkcounty_distorted.PNG>

Thank you very much,

---Mark

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

I'm not sure if this is the only issue, but the following line is not guaranteed
to do what you want, and in many cases it will definitely not do what you want:

table(xy.in <http://xy.in> <- inout(projection$lattice$loc,cbind(bound$loc[,1], bound$loc[,2])))

1) The inla.mesh.segment objects do not necessarily store the vertices of the curve in order.
2) bound$idx contains the information about which order to go through the vertices
3) even if the point were in order in loc, the code above would fail for curves with more
     than one connected component, which looks like exactly what you have.

If you found code on r-inla.org <http://r-inla.org> using the above, please let me know where so I can
 locate and modify it! Code elsewhere doing that would also be good to know about
even if I can't directly correct it.

To do this correctly you need to use your original SpatialPolygons object to do the
checking.  I believe rgeos::gIntersection can give you the wanted subset of points.

There is an alternate but also correct approach that only needs the inla package,
 but there is no ready-made function for it yet: the idea is to build a simple mesh with
the boundary with no extension:
simplemesh=inla.mesh.2d(boundary=bounds, max.edge=1e9)
ok = inla.mesh.projector(simplemesh, locations)$proj$ok
locations[ok,,drop=FALSE]

Please let me know if that approach works or not. If it does, I'll add a wrapper for it.
In the coming days& weeks, there will also be more and more Spatial object support
directly built into the mesh functions (the development version already lets you use
SpatialPolygons instead of inla.mesh.segment objects in most places).

Finn L, meshes-in-inla-developer

messages.body_plain:
Additionally, you can do it in the rgeneric framework. (see inla.doc('rgeneric'))

Here, you would fix the likelihood precision to a small value, and then define your own random effect N(0, sigma) to add on to the linear predictor.

What you would need to construct is the precision (inverse covariance) matrix for this new random effect as a function of two hyperparameters Gamma_0 and Gamma_1. I think this matrix would just be a diagonal, and therefore very easy to implement.

@Håvard: Maybe this would be a way to implement it for everyone in the future? (As a random effect with a fixed-noise likelihood.)

@CamDi: Personally, I would not try to construct a model with multiplicative noise as the first attempt at varying-noise-model. I would rather do sigma^2 = exp(Gamma1)^2 + exp(Gamma2*X)^2, or something similar, as my intuition is better on this additive noise model. In that case you could put the exp(Gamma1) into the usual Gaussian likelihood, and do exp(Gamma2*X) as the sigma in a random effect.

Kind regards,
Haakon Bakka

messages.body_plain:
Here's a wrapper function, and an example:

## Construct a model object for independent variables
##   N(0, sigma_i^2), i=1,...,n, where
##   log(sigma_i) = log(sigma0_i) + sum_{k=1}^p X_{ij} \theta_j
##   with independent priors  \theta_j ~ N(0, prec^{-1}), j=1,...,p, p >= 1
indep.sigma <- function(X, sigma0=1, prec=1e-8)
{
  n <- nrow(X)
  p <- ncol(X)
  ZeroM <- Diagonal(n, 0.0)
  UnitM <- Diagonal(n, 1.0)
  ZeroV <- matrix(0.0, n, 1)
  inla.spde2.generic(M0=ZeroM, M1=ZeroM, M2=UnitM,
                     B0=cbind(-log(sigma0), -X),
                     B1=ZeroV, B2=ZeroV,
                     theta.mu <http://theta.mu>=rep(0, p),
                     theta.Q=diag(rep(prec, p), p, p))
}

## Example:
## y_i ~ beta_0 + x_i beta_2 + N(0, sigma_i^2), where
## log(sigma_i) = \theta_1 + x_i \theta_2
library(INLA)
## Simulated data:
n <- 1000
data <- data.frame(x=rep(c(1, 2), each=n/2))
data$y <- 2 + 8*data$x + rnorm(n, sd=exp(0.3+data$x*0.6))
summary(data)
plot(data$y)

## Construct the inla model:
indep.sigma.model <- indep.sigma(X=cbind(1, data$x))
datalist <- c(as.list(data),
              list(noise=seq_along(data$x),
                   indep.sigma.model=indep.sigma.model))
formula <- y ~ +1 + x + f(noise, model=indep.sigma.model)

## Run inla, fixing the no longer needed measurement noise precision
to a large value:
result <- inla(formula, data=datalist, family="gaussian",
               control.family=list(hyper=list(
                                     prec=list(initial=log(1e9),
                                               fixed=TRUE))),
               verbose=TRUE)
summary(result)

messages.body_plain:
Hi,
I've rolled your 2nd email into this one, since it's the same question really.

<cut description of spatial field f with two observation sources with different variance>

> From paper <Bayesian Spatial Modelling with R-INLA> Section 3.3, I learn that INLA could model multiple likelihoods, simply by stacking two datasets.
> My question is what is the theory behind this easy manipulation? Will such manipulation change the model fitting, or the training of parameters of precision matrix?

This comes from basic statistical theory/methodology. Since the two data sources are considered conditionally independent given the "true" field f, the this combination of sources works the same as when combining the information from each individual data point; the total data likelihood is the product of each individual data point likelihood.

So it's not really a matter of _changing_ anything; this is simply the correct formulation of the theoretical problem in the practical inla code. But if you're wondering how the results will differ from doing two completely separate analyses, one for each data source; the joint analysis will give lower posterior uncertainty than each of the separate analyses, since the single field f will be informed by both sources of data. And this is exactly what is expected (and desired).

> Besides,  is it possible for INLA to estimate the noise variances for different sources ( iid zero-mean Gaussian distributed)  during model fitting?

Yes, as you noted above, one way is to format the data into a two column matrix, one for each likelihood (each row is NA for the "other" data source). I believe the paper lays out the technique for doing that with the help of inla.stack() for spatial models.

Finn Lindgren

messages.body_plain:
Hi Haakon and the INLA help group,

This is a bit of a delayed response following summer vacations and a renewed stab at making sense of this project.
First, thanks a lot for pointing me in the direction of the PC prior. It was a fair bit easier to make sense of than the previous parametrisations.
I've now spent a good amount of time experimenting with different values for Rho and sigma, and investigating how the resulting model fit behaves.
Unfortunately, the results are still troublesome.

Basically, I can make the model flip between having a covariate effect and a completely flat SPDE, and zero covariate effects with a SPDE that fits the observations near perfectly.  The only intermediate I’ve found is one where the spade is on the order of [0.99,1.01], i.e. plus or minus ~1 percent. Which is too small to have any real effect.

What bothers me is that I can’t understand how this solution can give a higher likelihood value than one which incorporates both covariates and SPDE. A regular regression type model  without side gives a fit that is, if not good, then at least explaining some of the variation in the observations, and the SPDE should then be able to take up the slack. It “feels” like incorporation the information inherent in the covariates should always lower the likelihood...

I've attached the code to this mail, in case anyone feels like having a look and see if we are making any glaringly obvious mistakes.
Alternatively, is there a different spatial model apart from the SPDE approach you would suggest as being a potential alternative?

All the best and thanks in advance,
Gustaf

On Tuesday, June 7, 2016 at 9:30:35 AM UTC+1, Haakon Bakka wrote:

> Hi Gustaf,
>
> If I understand you correctly, you want to penalise the complexity of the spde model. We have a new prior meant to do this, which has been successful in a couple of cases. I attach code for it here.
>
> Note: I would not say "the spde is too flexible",I would say "we use priors for the hyper-parameters that represents too flexible models". But maybe this is what you mean.
>
>
>
> local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new> = function(mesh, alpha=2, prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
> {
>   # Call inla.spde2.matern with range and standard deviation parametrization
>   d = INLA:::inla.ifelse(inherits(mesh, "inla.mesh"), 2, 1)
>   nu = alpha-d/2
>   kappa0 = log(8*nu)/2
>   tau0   = 0.5*(lgamma(nu)-lgamma(nu+d/2)-d/2*log(4*pi))-nu*kappa0
>   spde   = inla.spde2.matern(mesh = mesh,
>                              B.tau   = cbind(tau0,   nu,  -1),
>                              B.kappa = cbind(kappa0, -1, 0))
>
>   # Change prior information
>   param = c(prior.pc.rho, prior.pc.sig)
>   spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$prior = "pcspdega"
>   spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$param = param
>   spde$f$hyper.default$theta1$initial = log(prior.pc.rho[1])+1
>   spde$f$hyper.default$theta2$initial = log(prior.pc.sig[1])-1
>
>   # End and return
>   return(invisible(spde))
> }
>
>
> # And then call the function with
> sig0 = 1; rho0 = .3 #rho0 is typical range, sig0 typical sd
> # - YOU MUST SET rho0 , e.g. to half the length/width of your space
> # - You may reduce sig0 to have less spatial effect
> # - You may increase rho0 additionally, to make the spatial effect smoother
>
> spde = local.inla.spde2.matern.new <http://local.inla.spde2.matern.new>(mesh, prior.pc.rho = c(rho0, 0.5), prior.pc.sig = c(sig0, 0.5))
>
> # Taking out the spde
> If you have fitted the model with the spde, it is a bit difficult to "take out" the spde part and only think about the rest. This is because the (posterior) distribution of the spatial field is heavily correlated with the distributions of the fixed betas (in cases where you have spatial covariates). (I.e. feel free to do it, but be careful with interpretation)
>
> Example: The spatial field is sometimes heavily confounded with the intercept, but for predictions, this does not matter at all, since they are integrated out jointly.
>
> # Suggestions for evaluating the model
> In sample:
> - R2 with median posterior, for checing mean fit
> - Check how many of the points fall inside 95% credible intervals (marginally), for checking "uncertainty fit"
> - dic, waic (for checking Bayesian model fitness)
>
> Out of sample:
> - cpo (may take some time though) (for checking marginal out-of-sample fit, mean and uncertainty)
> - hold-out sets (corresponding to your desired "prediction scenarios")
>
> # code in the inla call
> ... control.compute = list(dic = TRUE, cpo=TRUE, waic = TRUE) ...
>
> # More
> I tried to answer your main questions. I hope you will ask further questions, or restate the ones you are the most interested in :)
>
>
> Kind regards,
> Haakon Bakka
>
>

> On 6 June 2016 at 23:47, Gustaf Rydevik <gustaf....@gmail.com> wrote:

> >
> >
> > Dear INLA group,
> >
> > we are developing a predictive spatial  poission model of deer,
> > using a combination of spatial and other covariates. We are assuming an SPDE-type spatial effect.
> > Fitting the model results in a very good R2 between predicted and observed deer counts.
> >
> > However, when we compare the prediction of the fixed effects only, removing the spatial effect, the R2 becomes incredibly low, on the order of 0.01 (see also the attached plot of predicted VS true deercount when including and excluding the spatial effect).  In comparison, a simple poisson regression excluding random effects gets an R2 of 0.06 - still not brilliant, but definitely better than the result of the INLA model.
> >
> > My guess is that the spde is "too flexible", exactly following the observed counts with no remaining variation to fit the other covariates to. Would this be a reasonable interpretation, and if so, how would you go about fixing it? After reading previous posts on here relating to SPDE models,  I've played around with the alpha, which doesn't affect anything, and with prior.variance.nominal. Prior.variance.nominal does do something, in that when it's set to 10^-7 or so, the SPDE becomes very slowly varying; but any lower than that, and the estimated random effects become "exact" again. A model without the SPDE leads to R2's of 0.25 or so...
> > Another approach I've been thinking about is to make the grid coarser, thereby forcing inla to average the effect of multiple data points, but I'm not if this is sensible.
> >
> >
> > On a tangential note, I am painfully aware that using R2 for model diagnostics on a spatial predictive poisson model is terribly abusive - any suggestions for better ways of evaluating/reporting model fit and predictive performance would be much appreciated!
> >
> >
> > Best regards,
> > Gustaf
> >
> >
> > Code here:

messages.body_plain:
On Tuesday, 16 August 2016 18:44:25 UTC+2, Gustaf Rydevik wrote:
> Hi Haakon and the INLA help group,
>
> This is a bit of a delayed response following summer vacations and a renewed stab at making sense of this project.
> First, thanks a lot for pointing me in the direction of the PC prior. It was a fair bit easier to make sense of than the previous parametrisations.
> I've now spent a good amount of time experimenting with different values for Rho and sigma, and investigating how the resulting model fit behaves.
> Unfortunately, the results are still troublesome.
>
> Basically, I can make the model flip between having a covariate effect and a completely flat SPDE, and zero covariate effects with a SPDE that fits the observations near perfectly.  The only intermediate I’ve found is one where the spade is on the order of [0.99,1.01], i.e. plus or minus ~1 percent. Which is too small to have any real effect.
>
> What bothers me is that I can’t understand how this solution can give a higher likelihood value than one which incorporates both covariates and SPDE. A regular regression type model  without side gives a fit that is, if not good, then at least explaining some of the variation in the observations, and the SPDE should then be able to take up the slack. It “feels” like incorporation the information inherent in the covariates should always lower the likelihood...
>
> I've attached the code to this mail, in case anyone feels like having a look and see if we are making any glaringly obvious mistakes.
> Alternatively, is there a different spatial model apart from the SPDE approach you would suggest as being a potential alternative?

Hi Gustav,

There are a couple of things that are puzzling me about the code. When you construct the mesh, you are using max.edge=c(10000, 400000), but when you are setting the prior you are using a tail probability P(rho < 0.25) = 0.50. If you are using that resolution for the mesh, your domain must span a very large spatial area and a range of 0.25 corresponds to a very high resolution and it would not be possible to resolve it on your chosen mesh. If your posterior estimate of the range is a lot smaller than your chosen max.edge, 10000, it is likely that the SPDE model is degenerating to something similar to an independent random effect and is acting a bit like an iid effect in your linear predictor. In which case it is quite natural that you are getting very good predictions if you check the model's ability to predict the data itself.

There are a couple of things you should check. First, you should take a look at the marginal posterior for range and see if it make sense compared to the resolution you have chosen in max.edge, and second, you could plot spatial maps of the marginal mean and standard deviations of the spatial effect and check if they look reasonable.

You should consider setting rho0 much higher like 20000 or 30000 or bigger in the prior specification. The specification P(rho < rho_0) = \alpha should make sense compared to the size of your domain.

--
Geir-Arne Fuglstad

Thanks Geir-Arne,

That was helpful - I remember being confused by whether Rho0 was measured in relative or absolute terms, and after trying both approaches assuming that it was relative. Thanks for setting me straight!
The dataset is measured in meters and covers Scotland, so the range is about 300 000 x 300 000. Given that, I assume that an Rho0 of 100k would be a sensible starting point? I think I still don't have a very clear intuitive understanding of what Rho actually means...
Tangentially, I just realised - in a poisson model, is the SPDE effect measured on the log scale, and thus multiplicative with the mean? if so, I guess a prior  sigma of log(1.1) or so should be reasonable (i.e 10% higher or lower than the predicted mean, on average)

Unfortunately, changing Rhos and Sigmas doesn't effect the actual results of the model, but identifying and removing the obvious misunderstandings are at least a step in the right direction (I'm getting a range of SPDE effects of +/- 5 on the log scale, fixed effects that are about 1, and an overall result that is quite clearly overfitting)

Best,
Gustaf

messages.body_plain:
Dear INLA experts,

I am using INLA to fit a random effects meta-analysis model as described here http://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC2667312/.

I think everything seems work and also I am comparing INLA results to another Bayesian method "bayesmeta" (https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/bayesmeta/vignettes/bayesmeta.html) to see the difference. I used same prior distributions for two approaches

When I plot the marginal density for the fixed effect, two results coincide well (I attached the plot). But when I plot the marginal density of the hyperparameter, INLA result has some awkward shape near to zero. I attached this plot with comparison of the bayesmeta approach (also I attached my R code to reproduce everything).

Then, I used "inla.hyperpar" function with different "dz" values to improve the estimates, and the resulting plot change a little bit, but I dont know.

My question is following is this normal to see such strange shape for marginal density of the hyperparameter obtained by INLA? Or should I find the right "dz" , "h" values for "inla.hyperpar" function?

Thank you very much for your help,

Best,

Burak

messages.body_plain:
HI Haakon, Geir-Arne, and others,

Thanks for all your feedback and suggestions so far! They've been most helpful, and the model is behaving a bit more sensibly now; though the fundamental oddity of relatively small fixed effects remain.

To summarise, these are the corrections I've now made in the model:

1) Rescaled the coordinates to measure distance in kilometers. the max edge parameter is now  max.edge=c(10, 400).
2) Switched to using the inla.spde2.pcmatern function that exists in the latest testing version of INLA
3) Adjusted the pc priors used so that prior.range=c(100,0.5), and prior.sigma=c(log(1.1),0.9).
I'm using a p=0.9 to attempt to put a stricter restriction on the standard deviation of the spde effect .

I've copied in the output of summary() at the end, based on fitting the model to 15000 observations. What I find notable is that the range parameter is ~19, compared to the prior of 100. According to our ecologist, this is in line with the scale at which one could expect to see deer density vary between ares of different suitability.
Depending on the exact values of the piors, the range parameter seem to vary from 7-20, but always be of the same order. The other thing is that the stdev parameter is ~2.5 (compared with the prior of log(1.1)=0.1 ). Again, this will vary slightly depending on the values  prior,
but seem to end up in a range of 2-5 or so. This stands out to me as being quite strange...
I've attached the log file of the model as requested  - I didn't see anything obviously weird there, but maybe you can find something.

Thanks again for the help - this list is definitely one of the big strengths of INLA!

Best regards,
Gustaf

Haakon

Hello,

I am wondering how to partition the whole dataset into CI subsets based on Markov property/precision matrix, while keeping the (most) necessary correlations between data points. And I am not very clear about the sentence in Section 3.1 "The ordering uses the Markov graph structure to divide the graph recursively into conditionally independent sets (Karypis and Kumar, 1999), which helps to make the Cholesky factor of the precision matrix sparse."  What I can understand is that the sparse Cholesky factor will have less fill-ins after nested dissection reordering (seems to be the case of Fig.6(a)). What I do not understand is that:

1) how to use "Markov graphs structure" of the mesh nodes to partition the whole 15182 nodes into CI-subsets?  Fig 6 seems to show the result after standard nested dissection reordering, while I could not understand in which step is Markov property utilized?

2) As Fig 6 shows, the arrow-shaped precision matrix indicates independence between even faraway entries. Is isn't it blocky diagonal precision matrix indicates the CI property?

3) why partitioning "recursively", instead of partition all subsets at one time? Is it standard graph partition algorithm in METIS?

4) Besides, does the sentence "for \kappa^2 = 16, corresponding to an approximate correlation range 0.7" means that only the neighboring nodes with correlations >=0.7 are kept?

Looking forward to your reply!

Thank you very much!

Kindly Regards
Liye

When re-running with inla.rerun, the results of summary(result) should not change much. (What you printed should also not change much, but the summary is even more interesting).

For the logfile you pasted:

Compute corrected stdev for theta[4]: negative 2.513880  positive 1.404846

Compute corrected stdev for theta[4]: negative 4.549782  positive 2.084138
Compute corrected stdev for theta[5]: negative 9.931343  positive 4.372232

These are big warning signs. When it corrects the stdev, the correction is with respect to it being 1. Here, the algorithm finds that the stdev was much bigger than it thought in both directions. I take this to mean that it probably did not manage to converge properly, i.e. it did not manage to find the correct posterior mode. I do not know what your theta4 and theta5 are, you see that from the summary, but I do believe that their posteriors are not correct.

The first thing I would do to fix this is to re-think the priors on these components. Compare them to the mean and sd of your dataset.

Kind regards,

On Sun, 2016-08-21 at 18:44 -0700, Sun Liye wrote:
> Hello,
>
> I am wondering how to partition the whole dataset into CI subsets
> based on Markov property/precision matrix, while keeping the (most)
> necessary correlations between data points. And I am not very clear
> about the sentence in Section 3.1 "The ordering uses the Markov graph
> structure to divide the graph recursively into conditionally
> independent sets (Karypis and Kumar, 1999), which helps to make the
> Cholesky factor of the precision matrix sparse."  What I can
> understand is that the sparse Cholesky factor will have less fill-ins
> after nested dissection reordering (seems to be the case of
> Fig.6(a)).

Hi Sun!

This is true, the idea is to reduce the ammount of fill-ins. I suggest
reading the appropriate section in the GMRF-book, which discuss all
these issues in detail and should provide answers to your questions.

Best wishes,
Håvard

>  What I do not understand is that:
>
> 1) how to use "Markov graphs structure" of the mesh nodes to
> partition the whole 15182 nodes into CI-subsets?  Fig 6 seems to show
> the result after standard nested dissection reordering, while I could
> not understand in which step is Markov property utilized?
>
> 2) As Fig 6 shows, the arrow-shaped precision matrix indicates
> independence between even faraway entries. Is isn't it blocky
> diagonal precision matrix indicates the CI property?
>
> 3) why partitioning "recursively", instead of partition all subsets
> at one time? Is it standard graph partition algorithm in METIS?
>
> 4) Besides, does the sentence "for \kappa^2 = 16, corresponding to an
> approximate correlation range 0.7" means that only the neighboring
> nodes with correlations >=0.7 are kept?
>
>
> Looking forward to your reply!
>
> Thank you very much!
>
> Kindly Regards
> Liye

On Sun, 2016-08-21 at 21:14 -0700, Thomas Suesse wrote:
> Hello users,
>
> consider the model
>
> z = Y  + e   (**)
>
> where Y is a Spatial lag model/SLM ( or also often called SAR) model
> and e is a measurement error, i.e. e_i ~ N( 0,sigma^2_e)
>
> INLA can fit a SLM (there is an example), but how do I fit an SLM
> with added measurement errors  according to (**) ?
>
> Regards
> Thomas

Hi,

this should be direct.

this line in the example (see inla.doc("slm"))

control.family = list(hyper=zero.variance)

simply fix this variance to a low value. just remove it, and you're
done.

H

messages.body_plain:
Hi!

The first you see is that the estimates of ''year'', ''year2'', ''x'', changes a lot. This could mean that the model is not well behaved in those parameters.

The first I would do is to check the parameters of the pc priors compared to the data standard deviation. (What is sd(cases)?)

The second thing is: Is there any components in your model that are modeling the same thing? Is your model in some way overspecified or not self-consistent?

So, I read inla.doc(''bym''), where it says: ''This model is simply a union of the besag model u and a iid model v, so that...''

You now have 3 IID components! Are you absolutely sure you want that? For me to check if that makes sense I will need to run the code.

Suggestion: Change from ''bym'' to model="besag", if that is what you wanted. Then you only have your own two iid effects

Kind regards,

Haakon Bakka

messages.body_plain:
Hello,

I would like to fit the following model using INLA:

Y_{1,i} ~Negbin(mu1,r)
Y_{2,i}~Negbin(mu2,r)
Y_{3,i}~Negbin(mu3,r)
Y_{4,i}~Negbin(mu4,r)

log(mu1)=log(n_i)+log(1-exp(-lambda_i 2^{rho_i}))
log(mu2)=log(n_i)+log(exp(-lambda_i 2^{rho_i})-exp(-lambda_i 10^{rho_i}))
log(mu3)=log(n_i)+log(exp(-lambda_i 2^{rho_i})-exp(-lambda_i 10^{rho_i}))
log(mu3)=log(n_i)+log(exp(-lambda_i 75^{rho_i}))

whereby lambda_i=beta1+beta2*age_i+beta3*I_weekend_i
and rho_i=beta4+beta5*age_i+beta6*I_weekend_i

and the log(n_i) is actually the offset.

Is it possible to do this and do you have any suggestions how to do it?
I have done a model with different linear predictors for each of the response categories, but I do not know how to adapt the formula to the above equations.

Kind regards,
Kim

Dear Havard,

Thank you for the suggestion.
I am fairly new to INLA and for sure to the rgeneric-function.
Looking at the documentation I see the rmodel has to follow some rules, but there are mainly 2 examples, so I am not entirely sure which rules.
And furthermore, is the cmd arguement something to be considered always?

Can I still combine a f() with the rgeneric model and an f(, model=iid4d) for example, or should all be wrapped in 1 function?

Kind regards,
Kim
